I have farmed these 8 mu for thirty years. I know every corner of this land. Here in Quzhou, the wheat-maize rotation is what feeds my family, and I do not intend to change what works. All 8 mu will go to winter wheat first, and then straight into summer maize after the June harvest. That is how we have always done it.

For the wheat, I will buy improved seed from the county supply store. Before sowing in October, I will run the rotary tiller to prepare the bed. I will spread compound fertilizer as a base and then top-dress with urea at green-up and again at jointing — about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu in total, plus phosphorus and potassium to keep the soil balanced. I will irrigate three times with my well: once after sowing if the autumn is dry, once in spring when the wheat greens up, and once at heading. I will spray herbicide once after sowing, and if I see aphids or rust, I will spray once more. If the weather is fair, I expect around 450 kg per mu.

For the maize, the window after wheat harvest is narrow, so I will plant hybrid seed directly into the stubble without tilling. No-tillage saves me labor and precious days. I will side-dress fertilizer at planting and again when the plants are knee-high — about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu. I will irrigate twice, usually around the big trumpet stage and again at filling if the summer turns hot and dry. I will spray for weeds once, and for corn borer if I see damage. With a good hybrid, I expect about 500 kg per mu.

Six people live in my household, and some of my children work off-farm, so labor is tight during harvest and planting. That is why no-tillage for maize suits me — my husband and I can manage the rush.
